title: Secure Quantum Handshakes: Quantum Network Verification Via Simon's Algorithm
authors: Reece Robertson, Sejal Patil, Sebastian Deffner
abstract: Quantum networking represents the future of secure communication, enabling fundamentally new capabilities through quantum information exchange. However, these networks require secure, high-fidelity quantum communication channels, and they require every participating node to be a genuine quantum device. Currently, there is no reliable method to verify whether clients entering a quantum network truly possess quantum computational capability and are connecting over robust channels. In this work, we introduce a client-validation protocol that functions as a proof-of-quantum-capability handshake. Our protocol secures a quantum network against classical spoofers, noisy quantum computers, and genuine quantum devices connecting with the network over noisy or insecure channels. We validate the efficacy of this protocol through numerical simulations under erasure, dephasing, and depolarizing noise models.
summary: This work presents a novel client-validation protocol for quantum networks that proves a node's genuine quantum computational capability. It achieves this by leveraging the exponential speedup of Simon's algorithm to solve a hidden-subgroup problem. The protocol is shown to secure the network against classical spoofers and noisy devices under various noise models.
main_problem: The paper addresses the critical need for a reliable method to verify that participating nodes in a quantum network are genuine quantum devices with high computational capability.
main_result: A client-validation protocol, based on Simon's algorithm, was developed that successfully admits only genuine, fault-tolerant quantum clients while rejecting classical or noisy quantum spoofers.
method: The protocol uses the inherent exponential separation between classical and quantum computation by requiring the client to solve a quantum-hard problem (Simon's problem) via an oracle query.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum network featuring a server (Guinevere) validating a client (Nimue) against classical and noisy adversaries. The core mechanism is the execution of Simon's period-finding algorithm.
key_observables: The primary observable is the success probability of recovering the hidden period/string, which must exceed a threshold to grant admission.
important_parameters: Noise parameters (erasure, dephasing, depolarizing) and the problem size $n$ are key parameters used to test the protocol's robustness.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the existence of a quantum server capable of running the oracle and relies on the quantum advantage of Simon's algorithm.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the concept of the verified quantum network, showing successful validation. Figure 3 details the networked circuit implementation of Simon's algorithm, and Figure 7 plots the success probability under depolarizing noise.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of client verification, details the protocol using Simon's algorithm in a networked setting, analyzes its resilience against various noise models via simulation, and concludes by discussing the implications for secure quantum communication.
why_interesting: While focused on networking, the rigorous analysis of noise thresholds (depolarizing channels) and the comparison to classical limitations provides valuable insights into the practical robustness required for any quantum information protocol.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Verified quantum network. An example of a verified quantum network constructed via our protocol. Here Guinevere represents a quantum server, Nimue a quantum client, Merlin a classical client, and Morgan le Fay a noisy quantum client. Through the protocol, Guinevere validates Nimue’s quantum capacity and admits her into the network. By the same token, Guinevere rejects Merlin and Morgan from the network when they fail to show fault-tolerant quantum capabilities.

FIG. 2. Simon’s algorithm. The circuit diagram for Simon’s algorithm. This circuit involves two n-qubit quantum registers collocated on a single quantum processor. The algorithm uses transversal measurements and Hadamard transformations. It also assumes access to a black-box unitary function Uf (|x1⟩|x2⟩) = |x1⟩|x2 ⊕f(x1)⟩which implements the unknown oracle of (1) and (2) as a reversible unitary operation for execution on a quantum device. At the conclusion of a fault-tolerant implementation of the algorithm, the bitstring measured in the top register will be a sample from (4). Both this and the following circuit diagrams were created using ⟨q|pic⟩[44].

FIG. 3. Networked Simon’s algorithm. A networked implementation of Simon’s algorithm; compare to the original version presented in Figure 2. In this version, three n-qubit quantum registers are used, one of which is controlled by a client device while the other two are controlled by a quantum server. The client prepares a superposition state which it sends to the server through a quantum channel, as denoted by the dashed SWAP gates. The server computes the oracle on the input and sends the result back to the client over the communication channel. The client may then prepare and sample from (4) as normal. This enables a situation in which the Simon oracle is implementable on the server yet...

FIG. 4. Network verification protocol. The commu- nication timeline diagram between Guinevere, the quantum server, and Nimue, the quantum client. The triangular ar- rows represent classical messages, and the diamond arrows represent quantum messages. The messages inside the box are repeated n + 20 times. Through this protocol, Guinevere is able to verify the fault-tolerant quantum capacity of Nimue.

FIG. 5. Admittance probability under an erasure channel. The results of a simulation of this protocol under a classical erasure noise model, which is typical of quantum communication via photons. The solution probability is plot- ted as a function of the problem size n over the strength of the noise channel p. As expected, we see ideal performance in the noiseless case, and we see the probability of success decay as both p and n increase.
